subject: Storage attach order, ephemeral vs block considerations & nodepool SLA

Subject: Storage attach order behavior and nodepool SLA implications

Hi Stephanie —

Thanks for the call earlier. To prepare our internal architecture review I attached an inventory of the IO patterns we're expecting (axion-io-requirements.xlsx). A couple of specific points we need clarification on before we sign off on the on-prem contract:

1) Attach order and failover: if a pod is scheduled onto a node that uses local NVMe for cache + remote block (RBD/iSCSI) for checkpoints, what's the observed attach-order behavior for rapid failover? Do we ever see the pod block waiting for network attach and miss our 60s cold-start SLO?

2) Ephemeral vs block: we want to use local NVMe for KV cache and a block-store for persistent checkpoints. Any guidance on eviction and rebind behavior across nodepools with different filesystem types (ext4 vs xfs) and mount options that might affect throughput during attach?

3) Nodepool SLA: we're trying to decide whether to buy the Reserved GPU/nodepool with higher SLA for critical traffic only. Need a clear mapping of availability impact vs attach latency trade-offs to present to procurement.

Can you share a short write-up and a recommended configuration we can hand to our infra team? Also, is there an attach-order design doc (CSI best practices) you suggest we review?

Appreciate it —
Jared Park
Platform Lead, Axion Health

Subject: Re: Storage attach order behavior and nodepool SLA implications

Hi Jared —

Thanks for the export and the clear bullets. Below is a concise summary with recommendations you can pass to your infra/procurement folks. I kept it focused on the attach-order and SLA trade-offs so procurement has the cost/impact points.

TL;DR: Use local NVMe for hot KV cache (ephemeral), RBD block PVs for checkpoints. Configure kubelet/CSI for delayed attach where possible; reserve a small pool of warm nodes (Reserved nodepool) to avoid cold-attach misses for the hottest replicas. Expect occasional 20–90s cold-attach windows for remote block (depends on CSI & network), but warm-node reuse cuts tail latency to <5s.

Details / recommendations:
- Attach ordering and cold-starts:
  - CSI remote block attaches typically involve: staging (node-level), publish (attach/mount), and filesystem resize. The slowest part is network attach + cloud/block-controller coordination. On-prem RBD over reliable datacenter networking usually finishes within 15–60s. Over congested links or heavy metadata ops it can spike to ~90s.
  - Mitigation: delayedAttach (CSI) + initContainer that waits for PV readiness avoids application-level timeouts; but it doesn't reduce absolute attach time. For hard SLOs, keep a warm buffer of nodes with pre-attached PVs (see below).

- Ephemeral (local NVMe) vs Block (network):
  - Local NVMe: excellent throughput, very low latency for KV cache. BUT data is ephemeral — use for in-memory/ephemeral caches only.
  - Block PV (RBD/iSCSI): necessary for durable checkpoints and replicas you need to rehydrate. Plan for throughput headroom (IOPS) and attach metadata load.
  - Filesystem: xfs tends to be more robust for concurrent metadata ops; ext4 is slightly faster in some small-RW patterns. Recommend xfs for checkpoint PVs and ext4 for ephemeral scratch if you prefer simplicity.

- Nodepool, eviction, and attach behavior:
  - Separate nodepools by role: cache-nodepool (local NVMe), checkpoint-nodepool (block-backed), and compute-nodepool (GPU/CPU). Taints + tolerations for strict placement.
  - Eviction policy: make checkpoint pods unmappable to cache-nodepool (use PodDisruptionBudget + PodTopologySpread to avoid correlated evictions).
  - Attach order: ensure your CSI implements node-level volume staging and you avoid multi-attach races by using unique topology keys per nodepool. We suggest using topology-aware storageclass with zone/host labels to minimize cross-host attach delays.

- SLA / procurement trade-offs:
  - Option A (lower cost): single mixed nodepool, no reserved capacity. Savings ~25–35% but expect cold-attach tail latencies during surges (20–90s).
  - Option B (recommended for critical traffic): Reserved nodepool (small warm buffer with pre-attached PVs) + autoscaler for burst. Cost premium ~8–12% for the reserved slice but reduces attach tail to <5s for warm replicas — this directly reduces perceived downtime and avoids application-level retries.

Next steps I can take if helpful:
- Draft one-page runbook for oncall/infra: attach order checks, CSI health probes, and a preattach script.
- Share Redwood's attach-order design doc: redwood-attach-order-design.pdf (attached).
- Work with Rishi to sketch the estimate for reserved pool sizing and cost delta for procurement.

Would you like the one-page runbook and a short cost delta sheet? We can also propose a two-week canary with instrumented metrics to measure attach tail percentiles in your environment.

Cheers,

Stef / Jared — quick follow-up from the ops/cost side. Adding here so procurement sees the sizing recommendation.

- Warm buffer sizing rule-of-thumb:
  - Keep warm nodes equal to 10–15% of peak critical replicas for the service you need under 5s attach. For Axion's numbers (see spreadsheet): that equates to ~6 warm nodes to start.
  - Warm nodes: pre-attach most used PVs at deployment time using our preattach job (we'll provide Helm hook).

- Cost delta: prototype-nodepool-sla.xlsx attached has a 12-month delta at three reserved sizes. If procurement wants a hard SLA commitment, recommend the medium reserved slice (12 nodes) to give headroom for surges and maintenance windows.

- Operational notes:
  - Instrument attach durations (CSI metrics + kubelet attach latency). We'll provide Grafana panels and an alert for P95 > 30s.
  - For the first rollout, run the canary in your staging rack with identical network path to production to validate sub-60s attaches.

If you want I can turn this into a short slide for procurement showing cost vs perceived downtime.

-rishi
Rishi Malhotra
Director, Deployment Engineering | Redwood Inference
